subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (1, −2, 3), (0, −1, 4) and (−2, 2, 1), then find (A′)⁻¹.

mark_split.label: Write A′ and find its determinant

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.101 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 150. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: classed SAQ on its length and shape — finding the inverse of a 3×3 matrix is Section B work on the real paper and matches Unit 3's SAQ answers 41-42. NOTE THE TENSION: the book prints no heading on p.101, so this answer falls inside the run of the p.100 heading "MATRICES-VSAQ", which would make it a 2-mark VSAQ. We overrule that, because the same bank puts answers 151 and 152 — both genuine VSAQ shapes — under a p.102 heading that reads only "MATRICES", so these page banners are chapter labels rather than reliable section markers. This classification is OURS. Printed appearances: none — this answer carries no year tag. The dash and the inverse can be done in either order: (A′)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)′. Taking the transpose FIRST is chosen here because it costs one line and the cofactors then follow the ordinary route. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular 1x7 for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Write A′ and find its determinant
steps.margin_note: First mark. Transpose first — rows become columns — then take the determinant. Transposing never changes a determinant, so |A′| = |A|.
steps.memory_tip: Transpose FIRST, then take the determinant — though transposing never changes it.

recall.must_convey: That A′ is written by exchanging rows and columns, and |A′| = 1, which is non-zero.
accept: transpose A then take the determinant which is one
the transpose has the rows and columns swapped and its determinant is one
find A dash and its determinant
A transpose teeskoni determinant kanukovali, one vasthundi
the determinant is one so the inverse exists

steps.why: A determinant is unchanged by transposing, so |A′| could equally be found from A. Either route gives 1.
common_mistakes: Reversing the rows instead of exchanging rows with columns.

steps.label: Find the cofactor matrix
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Nine 2×2 determinants with the sign board + − + / − + − / + − +.
steps.memory_tip: Nine 2×2 determinants with the sign board + − + / − + − / + − +.
lines: Deleting each entry’s row and column and applying

recall.must_convey: That the nine cofactors of A′ are computed with the correct signs.
accept: find the nine cofactors using the minors and the sign board
delete each row and column, take the two by two, apply the sign
nine cofactors sign board tho kanukovali

steps.why: The cofactors are of A′, not of A — transposing first means everything after it is ordinary, with no extra bookkeeping.
common_mistakes: Computing the cofactors of A instead of A′.

steps.label: Transpose and divide
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The adjoint is the cofactor matrix transposed; dividing by |A′| = 1 leaves it unchanged.
steps.memory_tip: The adjoint is the cofactor matrix transposed; dividing by 1 leaves it unchanged.

recall.must_convey: That the adjoint is the transposed cofactor matrix and, since |A′| = 1, that is the inverse.
accept: transpose the cofactor matrix to get the adjoint and divide by one
the determinant is one so the adjoint is the inverse
transpose then divide by the determinant
cofactor matrix transpose chesi one tho divide cheyyali

steps.why: Two transposes appear in this question — one on A at the start and one on the cofactor matrix at the end. They are unrelated, and both are required.
common_mistakes: Dividing by |A| when it is not 1.

insider_note: Transpose FIRST and then invert that — the cofactors of A′ are not the cofactors of A rearranged. |A′| = 1, so the inverse is simply the adjoint.
